segments.speaker: omar
segments.narration_text: OMAR: Our purpose is simple to say and hard to do: we help people live longer, healthier, happier lives, including people who are well today. Our mission is to be the world's most customer-centric healthcare company. In practice, every role asks one question: did this help the patient? Our goal follows from that: outstanding patient experience, alongside excellent clinical outcomes. Honestly, my first week here, I felt there was too much to take in. You don't need to remember everything today — just where to find it.

segments.speaker: omar
segments.narration_text: OMAR: Every clinic has values on a wall. Ours only matter if you can see them in what people do. Collaborative: we act together, treat everyone with respect, and stay transparent. Responsible: own your decisions, make things happen, and hold each other to the same standard. Ambitious: go above and beyond, and challenge the status quo when it stops serving patients. Caring: act with empathy, because everyone matters. As you go on, think which of these you already do without being asked.

segments.speaker: omar
segments.narration_text: OMAR: Strategy feels like someone else's job until you find your own work inside it. Here are the seven pillars. Closer: convenient access — clinics, community clinics and home health care, digital services, telemedicine. Cure: the best Saudi doctors, clinical outcomes, centres of excellence, prevention and wellbeing. Capabilities: a repeatable model for running and growing clinics, with real governance. Culture: our mission and values, servant leadership, a culture of excellence. Clinicians: a caring environment, competitive benefits, room to grow. Care: seamless experience, empathy, loyalty built through My Care. Cost: competitive cost to serve. Whichever one you picked, that's your line in.

segments.narration_text: OMAR: Who do we serve? First, patients and their families — sick or healthy. Many of the people who walk in today are well, and we want them to stay that way. Second, the community around each clinic. Third, corporates and insurers. Three groups, one standard.

segments.speaker: omar
segments.narration_text: OMAR: We opened our first clinic in North Jeddah in 2017. In 2019 we started the employment check-up unit, our first corporate service. Then came East Jeddah, the dental centre, and Petro-Rabigh in 2023, our first clinic inside a corporate community. Riyadh followed in 2024, a flagship to put the brand on the map. The last two years added our first community clinics. Nine years, nine steps, one idea: bring good care closer.

segments.speaker: omar
segments.narration_text: OMAR: Four values sit under everything. Respect — the rights, privacy and dignity of patients, families and colleagues. Integrity — be transparent, and disclose any conflict of interest. Accountability — a culture where people report safety concerns instead of staying quiet. Innovation and collaboration — research and community work that improves outcomes. And the rule you'll use: faced with an ethical dilemma, complete an incident report within twenty-four hours and bring in the ethics team. You're never expected to work it out alone.

segments.narration_text: OMAR: Nine types. Open the ones you need. Annual: after probation, five days carried over, used by end of March. Sick: valid report needed. First thirty days paid in full. Work injury covers commuting, and has a same-day or next-day deadline. Maternity: twelve weeks, starting up to four weeks early. Exam leave: academic exams only, documents two weeks ahead. Scientific: by profession, and can't be carried over. Hajj: two years' service and a permit. Compassionate: marriage, paternity, bereavement. Then Eid, Founding Day, National Day. We'll practise the four people ask about most.

segments.speaker: omar
segments.narration_text: OMAR: One example, properly. A colleague is off sick forty days in a year, with valid reports. First, she tells her line manager — that's first, not last. The first thirty days are paid in full. Ten days fall into the next band, and that's where pay drops. Note the detail people miss: it's the total in the year that sets the band, not one spell. Beyond ninety days it's unpaid. And if the report is from outside My Clinic, the Staff Health Clinic must approve it. Now: what changes if her report comes from another hospital?

segments.narration_text: OMAR: GOSI is the General Organization for Social Insurance — the government body for social protection in Saudi Arabia. It applies to Saudi employees, until retirement at sixty. The split matters: you pay nine point seven five per cent of basic plus housing. My Clinic pays eleven point seven five. So the real contribution is twenty-one point five, and most of it isn't yours.

Apply your rate, nine point seven five per cent. The company's rate never touches your payslip. Six thousand times nought point nought nine seven five is five hundred and eighty-five riyals a month. That's the line to look for.

segments.speaker: omar
segments.narration_text: OMAR: One caveat before the numbers: whether you're eligible for overtime at all depends on your grade. Check that first. Now the arithmetic. Basic six thousand. Divide by thirty days times eight hours — two hundred and forty hours — and you get twenty-five riyals an hour. On a normal working day, multiply by one and a half. That's thirty-seven riyals fifty. On a public holiday, multiply by two. Fifty riyals an hour. Same hourly rate both times. Only the multiplier moves.

# Voice-over script — MC03-welcome-on-board

Language: en · Pace: ~140 wpm · Two voices: **Dr. Omar** (lead host) and **Noor** (co-host) — [`companions.md`](../../00_program/characters/companions.md) §5.

## Voices

| Voice | Brief | Lines in this module | Provider / voice id |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Dr. Omar** (`OMAR:`) | Male, late 30s, friendly, confident and relaxed; international English with a light Gulf Arabic accent welcome; medium-low pitch; ~140 wpm | 35 | Pending program **D10** |
| **Noor** (`NOOR:`) | Female, early-to-mid 30s, warm, calm and clear; international English with a light Gulf Arabic accent welcome; smiling but not bubbly; ~140 wpm | 4 | Pending program **D10** |

Neither voice may be cloned from, or resemble, a real My Clinic employee. Record a 30-second sample of each voice reading a “meet your guide” line for approval before producing this module. Once D10 closes, record the provider and voice ids in `00_program/narration-and-lexicon.md` §1 and in `narration-script.json` → `voice`.

The speaker label (`OMAR:` / `NOOR:`) selects the voice and is **not** spoken; `tts_text` in [`audio-script-export.json`](audio-script-export.json) already has it removed and the lexicon applied. Two-voice screens are recorded as one file per `part` and joined with 0.3 s of silence (companions.md §5).
